blocks.text: Penicillin is a powerful antibiotic used to treat many kinds of bacterial infection, such as respiratory infections like strep throat, pneumonia, scarlet fever and sinusitis. It also helps to treat skin and soft-tissue infections such as cellulitis and erysipelas.

The structure of penicillin contains two core rings: a four-membered beta-lactam ring and a five-membered thiazolidine ring, both with side chains attached. The beta-lactam ring is crucial for the antibiotic's activity; it is also the site where bacterial enzymes called beta-lactamases can attack and deactivate penicillin.

blocks.alt: Skeletal structure: a four-membered ring (C, C, N and a C=O carbon) fused at the N and the next carbon to a five-membered ring containing S, a carbon with two methyl lines, and a carbon bearing a hashed bond to C(=O)OH. The top-left ring carbon carries a solid wedge to N-H, which is bonded to a C=O group bearing R; the ring-fusion carbon carries a hashed bond to H. R is pink, N purple, H blue, S green and O red.
blocks.caption: Figure 32.2: Chemical structure of Penicillin (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 32.2).

blocks.text: The structure of penicillin looks identical to the amino acid sequence of the enzyme which strengthens the cell wall. The enzyme takes up the penicillin molecule, the beta-lactam ring opens, and penicillin binds permanently to the enzyme, which is inactivated. The bacteria keep growing, but without a functional cell wall they eventually burst and die. Human cells have no cell wall, so penicillin does not harm our cells.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Penicillin resembles the enzyme's normal substrate (the D-Ala-D-Ala end of the cell-wall building block), not the enzyme's own amino acid sequence; the enzyme takes penicillin for its substrate.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin by accident when he noticed that mould growing on a contaminated petri dish had killed the surrounding bacteria. The mould, later identified as Penicillium, released a substance that stopped bacterial growth. This chance observation led to the first antibiotic and changed modern medicine.
